ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is an AC generator, connected to the primary coil of the transformer; in the primary-side circuit there is ammeter A1, and voltmeter V1 is connected in parallel across the two ends of the primary side. On the right side is the secondary coil, which is drawn as a vertical winding, with the lower end connected into the lower wire of the secondary side; contact P touches a certain position of the secondary coil from the right side and is connected to the upper wire of the secondary side, so the number of turns actually connected into the secondary side is the number of turns between contact P and the lower end of the secondary coil. In the secondary-side circuit, ammeter A2 is in the upper branch, voltmeter V2 is connected in parallel at the secondary-side output end, and the user load and the transmission-line resistance R0 are connected in series in the secondary-side loop; therefore A2 measures the secondary-side current passing through the user and R0. Reasoning: A decrease in the reading of V1 means that the voltage U1 across the two ends of the primary coil decreases. The user load remains unchanged, and R0 also remains unchanged; if the reading of A2 is to be kept unchanged, that is, the current in the secondary-side loop is to be kept unchanged, then the voltage across the user and the voltage drop across R0 both remain unchanged, and therefore the secondary-side supply voltage U2 should also remain unchanged. An ideal transformer satisfies U2/U1 = n2/n1; the number of turns n1 of the primary coil remains unchanged, and when U1 decreases, to keep U2 unchanged, the effective number of turns n2 of the secondary coil must be increased. From the figure it can be seen that when contact P moves upward, the number of turns included between P and the lower end of the secondary coil increases, so contact P should be moved upward appropriately.
